pages.bodyText: Home / Resources / Engineering Guides / From prototype screw to repeat production: a stage-gate handover guide Engineering Guides From prototype screw to repeat production: a stage-gate handover guide An approved sample is an important milestone, but it is not the whole production plan. A prototype may answer a geometry question while leaving material, treatment, packaging or repeat-lot controls unresolved. This guide sets out practical approval gates for moving a custom fastener into repeat purchasing. Its purpose is to make the meaning of each approval visible, so that engineering, purchasing and the supplier do not interpret the same sample differently. Theo Wan · 2026-10-30 Gate 1: define what the prototype must prove Gate 2: freeze the information needed to manufacture Gate 3: agree the sample schedule and dependencies Gate 4: review samples against the agreed evidence Gate 5: confirm the repeat-production route Gate 6: release the production control package Gate 7: manage the first repeat order as a learning point Gate 8: define when the approval must be revisited Gate 1: define what the prototype must prove State the questions the first parts are intended to answer. They may concern tool access, assembly clearance, locating geometry, retained movement or the feasibility of a proposed route. Identify which material and surface conditions must already be representative and which are provisional. If the prototype is intended only for a fit check, record that limit. Do not allow a convenient early sample to become an implied approval of properties or treatment that were never evaluated. Give each question an owner and an acceptance decision. The customer’s equipment designer should own assembly-level requirements and approve changes to the interface. The supplier should state manufacturing assumptions and exceptions. If a test or document is required, agree its scope and availability before committing to the sample programme. This avoids a late discovery that the chosen sample condition cannot answer the intended acceptance question. Gate 2: freeze the information needed to manufacture Confirm the part number, drawing revision, mating references, material and condition, treatment scope, functional dimensions and inspection requirements. Resolve conflicts between models, drawings and samples. If a manufacturing proposal changes a feature, obtain written approval through the controlled definition. Do not rely on an informal photograph or an untracked annotation to communicate a production change. Define the scope of tooling or setup approval. A forming tool, special drive tool or dedicated inspection arrangement can depend on features that are still being refined. Ask which changes would require rework or a new approval cycle. Make those dependencies visible to the project planner. The cheapest route for a frozen drawing may not be the most practical route for a design that is still undergoing substantial revision. Gate 3: agree the sample schedule and dependencies Separate drawing approval, material availability, tooling, secondary operations, treatment and verification. State when the agreed sampling period begins and what customer decisions are required during it. ZUFEK typically discusses approximately 10–15 days for tooling and sampling, subject to technical review and confirmation. That is not a blanket lead-time guarantee for every material, treatment or documentation requirement. Repeat-production delivery is agreed separately. Record what happens if the drawing changes during sampling. A revised interface may invalidate a tool, a sample or part of the planned evaluation. The project should decide whether to continue with the old revision for a limited question or stop and restart against the new definition. Do not let two revisions proceed under one approval label without identifying which result belongs to each. Gate 4: review samples against the agreed evidence Check the loose part against the drawing and the inspection plan. Review the material and treatment basis where those are part of the sample scope. If assembly evaluation is needed, identify the mating components and the question being answered. A part that passes a dimensional report may still require a defined assembly check; an assembly that seems to fit does not establish every material or dimensional requirement. Create a sample decision record with accepted, rejected or conditionally accepted status for each open issue. Conditional approval needs a stated limitation and a closure action. For example, approval of a geometry sample before final treatment should name the outstanding treatment review. Avoid a single “sample OK” message that later teams interpret as approval of every possible delivery condition. Gate 5: confirm the repeat-production route The sample route and intended production route may differ. If a turned prototype will become a formed or hybrid part, review how the critical interfaces and required properties will be preserved. Identify which checks or approvals need repeating. A common nominal drawing is not, by itself, evidence that every route change is irrelevant to the delivered part. Confirm the quantity assumptions behind the production quotation, including tooling, secondary operations, treatment, inspection, documents and packaging. Discuss the effect of smaller repeat orders or a different order pattern. Separate manufacturing readiness from purchasing readiness: a supplier can be capable of making the part while the programme still lacks an approved inspection plan or release reference. Gate 6: release the production control package The package should contain the approved drawing and revision, route assumptions or approved exceptions, material and treatment requirements, inspection plan, sample approval, lot identification and packaging instructions. Identify who can approve later deviations and which changes require notification. Keep the package accessible to the teams placing repeat orders rather than only to the engineer who handled the first sample. Define the records that accompany a shipment and the identifiers that connect them to the physical parts. If lots can be split or repacked, agree how that link will be maintained. Where variants look alike, design the labels and receiving instructions to prevent mixing. An elegant sample does not compensate for a production arrangement that cannot distinguish revisions during stores handling. Gate 7: manage the first repeat order as a learning point Review whether the delivered parts, documents, packaging and schedule match the released scope. Record any ambiguity found by receiving or assembly teams and resolve it through the controlled package. Do not quietly normalise an exception because the first shipment has already arrived. A small clarification at this stage can prevent the same problem from appearing in every later order. Keep assembly observations separate from unverified performance claims. If a customer reports an issue, identify the part, revision, lot, installation condition and supporting evidence before drawing conclusions. The response may involve a component requirement, a mating-part issue or an installation procedure. A structured review is more useful than assuming that every problem is caused by the fastener or that a successful first assembly proves every future condition. Gate 8: define when the approval must be revisited A change in material, treatment, route, supplier source, drawing or mating assembly may affect the approved basis. Define the notification and reapproval expectations in advance. Some changes may need a limited document review; others may need new samples or appropriate evaluation. Record the decision and its permitted scope. Do not assume that an old approval is either universally permanent or automatically invalid after every administrative change. Use a handover record with fields for gate, required input, evidence, owner, decision, open action and approval reference. Release the next gate only when its dependencies are understood. The goal is a maintainable production definition that survives personnel changes and repeat orders. A prototype becomes useful production knowledge when the team preserves what it proved, what it did not prove and the conditions under which its approval remains valid. Sources and scope Source context is distinguished from ZUFEK editorial analysis. Examples are illustrative, not delivered customer cases or measured test results. pages.bodyText: Home / Resources / Custom fastener FAQ TECHNICAL INSIGHTS Custom fastener FAQ Answers to common purchasing and engineering questions before requesting drawing-defined metal screws. Product-specific decisions still follow the approved drawing, quantity and agreed acceptance requirements. Drawings and quotations What information is needed for a useful custom screw quotation? Send the current drawing revision, quantity and expected repeat demand, application, required material and surface condition, critical dimensions and inspection or document requirements. Include the mating-part relationship when the screw locates, pivots, retains or seals with another component. If information is not yet fixed, identify the open questions rather than let each supplier make a different assumption. Can you work from a sample or a photograph? A sample or clear photograph can help start a discussion, but it does not establish hidden geometry, material condition, tolerances or performance requirements. The team must clarify those details and confirm a controlled drawing or specification before production. A similar external appearance is not evidence that two parts will be interchangeable in the intended assembly. Is there one minimum order quantity for every custom part? No single quantity is promised for all custom screws. Feasibility and the practical order quantity depend on geometry, material, tooling, route, treatment and the requested evidence. State the prototype quantity and expected production demand so that the team can review a suitable proposal. A minimum or economic quantity quoted for one design should not be applied to another without review. Samples and manufacturing How long do tooling and samples normally take? Tooling and sampling are typically discussed at approximately 10–15 days, subject to drawing review and confirmation of the sample specification. Material availability, special treatment and required verification can affect the agreed schedule. Confirm the start milestone in the quotation. Repeat-production delivery is quoted separately and is not automatically the same as the sampling period. Should a custom screw be cold headed or CNC turned? The route depends on the drawing, material, quantity and final acceptance requirements. Turning can be reviewed for complex geometry and flexible development quantities; forming or a hybrid route can be evaluated for suitable repeat-production programmes. Ask for route assumptions and a complete comparison including tooling, secondary operations, treatment and inspection. Neither process name alone proves a finished part will meet its requirements. Can the geometry change after sample approval? Changes should follow a controlled review. Identify the affected drawing revision, functional interfaces, tooling, route and evidence. The customer’s responsible approver must accept a proposed change before it is treated as the production definition. A previous sample approval should not be interpreted as permission for an unreviewed substitution in material, treatment or geometry. Materials and surface treatment Does a material grade establish the finished screw strength? A raw material designation is not, by itself, the complete finished-property requirement. Grade, material condition, manufacturing route and relevant treatment must be considered with the actual specification. State the required finished properties and evidence separately from the raw grade. Do not assume that every screw described with the same material family has the same delivered strength or service suitability. Can I request a different material if availability changes? An alternative can be reviewed, but it must be approved against the actual interface and requirements. Compare the material condition, finished properties, treatment, dimensions, manufacturing route and documentation. A familiar cross-reference or a higher nominal strength does not automatically establish equivalence. Keep approved alternatives and any limitations identifiable on the drawing, order or deviation record. Which coating should I choose for outdoor equipment? The correct review needs the actual exposure, mating materials, required protection, assembly behaviour and acceptance evidence. Colour alone is not a specification. Define treatment scope and final dimensions, especially for threads and close-fitting shoulders. A corrosion-test result on a loose fastener is not a universal prediction of field life for the installed joint. Inspection and acceptance Does CCD inspection check every property of a screw? No. A suitable vision setup can check accessible dimensions and visible profiles within its agreed scope. It does not independently establish material strength, coating chemistry, hidden geometry or every three-dimensional relationship. Thread gauges, dimensional measurements, material or treatment records and any required assembly checks should be selected for the actual drawing and failure risks. Are all custom screws inspected on every characteristic on every piece? Inspection scope and frequency must be agreed. First-article checks, lot sampling and every-piece sorting answer different needs. If every-piece checking is required, name the characteristic, method and criteria. Do not interpret an optical sort of selected external features as proof that every property of every part has been measured. Can you provide material and inspection documents? Specify the exact documents and tests needed during quotation. Availability, traceability, testing arrangements and cost or schedule implications must be confirmed for the part. A generic data sheet is different from a record tied to a delivered lot. The website does not claim a certification, test result or document package that has not been confirmed for the actual order. Ordering, delivery and information How can repeat orders use the same approved specification? Order against the controlled part number and drawing revision, retain the approved sample and acceptance record, and agree notification requirements for relevant changes. Identify material, finish, inspection, packaging and lot-label expectations. A repeat order should preserve the approved interface rather than rely only on a familiar part description or an old photograph. Does an application study on this website describe a delivered customer project? Application studies are illustrative design reviews unless explicitly supported and identified otherwise. They explain how a team might connect an assembly need with geometry, materials, process and validation. They do not claim measured customer results, OEM approval or a specific delivered programme. ZUFEK’s automotive background refers to component supply-chain projects, not an unsupported direct OEM endorsement. Where should I send a drawing or follow up an inquiry? Use the request-a-quote form or email info@zufek.net . Include the drawing revision and quantity. If you have already submitted a form successfully, keep its inquiry reference and include it when following up. A saved inquiry and an email notification are separate steps; a submission acknowledgement is not a quotation or acceptance of an order. RFQ checklist · Request a quote
